openers.founders-and-pioneers: Soil science has founders, and many of them came to it from somewhere else. A German lawyer and land tax assessor born in 1794 is considered one of them; a Russian geologist and geographer born in 1846 is credited with laying the field's foundations. Chemists and microbiologists followed: a German who helped found organic chemistry, a Dutch botanist who helped found virology, a Ukrainian and Russian microbiologist who pioneered the cycle-of-life concept. Americans carried the work into the 20th century, from the man who ran the national soil survey from 1913 until his death to a leading soil physicist and the scientist who first built the USDA's Soil Taxonomy. This chapter meets them one by one, starting with {{ref:soil-hist-001}}.

soil-hist-001.title: Vasily Dokuchaev, who saw soil as a natural body
soil-hist-001.text: Chernozem, podsol, gley and solonets are Russian words, and they entered the world's soil vocabulary through one man's research. Vasily Dokuchaev (1846–1903) was a Russian geologist and geographer credited with laying the foundations of soil science. He is commonly called its father. He was perhaps the first to investigate different soil types across broad geographic areas. After extensive field studies of Russian soils in 1883 he reached his theory, and his most famous work, {{ref:soil-hist-002}}, appeared that same year. Soil, he argued, is a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock beneath it. Climate, vegetation, parent material, relief and age turn that bedrock into soil. Parent material alone could not explain why soil types vary from place to place. Climate, topography and the length of soil formation mattered too. On these ideas he built the very first soil classification, which described five factors of soil formation. His output was vast: from 1869 to 1901 he published 285 works, including 61 books and 4 maps. Many soil scientists took up his ideas, {{ref:soil-hist-010}} among them. The IUSS's Dokuchaev Award, likened to a Nobel Prize for soil science, honors him.

soil-hist-004.title: Justus von Liebig brings chemistry to the farm
soil-hist-004.text: In 1840 a German chemist argued that chemistry could revolutionize farming. Justus von Liebig (1803–1873) was a principal founder of organic chemistry and made major contributions to agricultural and biological chemistry. His book Organic Chemistry in its Application to Agriculture and Physiology was widely translated, fiercely criticized and highly influential. Critics pointed to his inexperience in practice. Even so, his writings spurred agricultural experiment and debate in Germany, England and France. He stressed nitrogen and minerals as essential plant nutrients and popularized the law of the minimum, earning the name "father of the fertilizer industry." Around 1840 he suggested dissolving animal bones in sulfuric acid to make fertilizer, a process first used in Britain in 1841. The early idea of soil as a store of plant nutrients rested on his thinking. Seeing both synthesis and decay in living systems, he also became an early advocate of conservation, including recycling sewage.

soil-hist-010.title: Hans Jenny gives soil formation its variables
soil-hist-010.text: Hans Jenny (1899–1992) made the study of soil formation quantitative. The Swiss-born soil scientist was an expert in pedology, above all in the processes that form soils. He took a doctorate at ETH Zurich in 1927 on ion exchange reactions and joined the University of California, Berkeley, in 1936. International recognition followed his 1941 book Factors of Soil Formation: A System of Quantitative Pedology. It combined field studies with the formalism of physical chemistry. Soil properties were tied to climate, biota, relief, parent material and time, with room for further variables, the idea behind {{ref:soil-form-049}}. In 1980 he recast the factors as state variables and extended their effects to whole ecosystems. His factors underlie the CLORPT model of soil-landscape modelling and the scorpan approach of digital soil mapping. He studied the Mendocino pygmy forest, whose stunted plants grow on a 500,000-year-old marine terrace; a reserve there bears his name. In his 1980 article "Alcohol or Humus" he argued against turning crop residues and forest humus into fuel. That would curtail carbon and nitrogen cycles and speed the oxidation of humus. In 1949 he was President of the {{ref:soil-hist-048}}.

soil-hist-013.title: Sergei Winogradsky takes microbes out of the clinic
soil-hist-013.text: Sergei Winogradsky (1856–1953) was among the first to study microbes outside medicine, which makes him an early student of microbial ecology. The Ukrainian and Russian microbiologist, ecologist and soil scientist pioneered the cycle-of-life concept. He discovered several biogeochemical cycles and parts of them. In 1887 he found that Beggiatoa oxidizes hydrogen sulfide as an energy source, the first known form of lithotrophy. From 1888 in Zürich he identified the bacteria behind nitrification. Nitrosomonas and Nitrosococcus oxidize ammonium to nitrite; Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate. He described this two-step process in 1890. He also identified Clostridium pasteurianum, a free-living anaerobe that fixes atmospheric nitrogen without living in legume root nodules. From 1922 he led the Pasteur Institute's agricultural bacteriology division, studying iron and nitrifying bacteria, Azotobacter, cellulose decomposers and ways to culture soil microbes. His student Vasily Omelianski spread his concepts and methods in the Soviet Union in the following decades.

soil-hist-003.title: Friedrich Fallou, the tax assessor who named pedology
soil-hist-003.text: A land tax assessor gave soil science one of its names. Friedrich Albert Fallou (1794–1877) was a German lawyer who spent most of his career evaluating forest and farmland for Saxony. The work worried him. Soil quality was declining, and he began relating soil profiles to how they formed. His First Principles of Soil Science (1857) and Pedology or General and Special Soil Science (1862) turned his field observations into a system. The 1862 book proposed a way to describe soil profiles, discussed soils' physical and chemical properties and classified soils by their minerals. That year he argued that soil was separate in nature from geology. He introduced the term pedology to found soil study as an independent science. Pedology described soil regardless of plants or use; agrology studied soil in relation to plants and farming. Dokuchaev proved more influential. Still, {{ref:soil-hist-008}} regarded Fallou as the founder of modern soil science, and Yarilov's 1904 article called him "Founder of Soil Science".

soil-hist-016.title: Martinus Beijerinck, from root nodules to viruses
soil-hist-016.text: In 1898 filtration experiments led Martinus Beijerinck to a striking conclusion: tobacco mosaic disease is caused by an agent smaller than a bacterium. He named it a virus. The Dutch microbiologist and botanist (1851–1931) is counted among the founders of virology and of environmental microbiology. In soil, his work centered on nitrogen fixation. He revealed the symbiosis between legumes and the nodule bacteria that fix nitrogen, a reaction vital to soil fertility and agriculture. He fully described the process found by Hellriegel and Wilfarth, and in 1901 showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes atmospheric nitrogen. He also discovered bacterial sulfate reduction. In it, bacteria use sulfate instead of oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, the final receiver of electrons in their energy-yielding chemistry. He isolated the first known sulfate-reducing bacterium, now called Desulfovibrio desulfuricans. He invented {{ref:soil-hist-017}} and founded the Delft School of Microbiology. The maxim "everything is everywhere, but the environment selects" is often credited to him, but it was Lourens Baas Becking's.

soil-hist-008.title: Konstantin Glinka carries Russian soil science west
soil-hist-008.text: For years a language barrier kept Russian soil science from Western Europe. Konstantin Glinka (1867–1927) broke through it. A student of Dokuchaev, he did geological and soil research under him from 1889, including work in Poltava and on the Forest Department expedition. His 1908 soil science textbook included the first schematic soil map of the world. His German publication of 1914 finally carried the Russian team's work west, and {{ref:soil-hist-009}} translated a version from German into English. Glinka became the first director of the Dokuchaev Soil Science Institute and wrote over 150 works on soil, geography, mineralogy and geology. By the 1920s he had found Russian soils that did not fit present climates; they were seen as relics of warmer past climates. In 1927 he became the first soil scientist elected to the USSR Academy of Sciences. That year he also led the Soviet delegation to the First International Congress of Soil Scientists in Washington.

soil-hist-007.title: Eugene Hilgard puts climate into American soil science
soil-hist-007.text: In 1860, in Mississippi, Eugene W. Hilgard studied how rock material, climate and vegetation relate to the type of soil that develops. The German-American expert on pedology (1833–1916) is considered the father of modern soil science in the United States. He was an authority on climate as a soil-forming factor, on soil chemistry and on the reclamation of alkali soils. From 1875 to 1904 he was professor of agricultural chemistry at the University of California, Berkeley, and directed the state agricultural experiment station. For the Northern Transcontinental Survey of 1881–1883 he studied soils of the southwestern states and the Pacific slope. He related them to geology, composition, native flora and farming. His 1892 Relations of Climate to Soils won the Liebig medal in 1894. With his 1906 book Soils, it established climate as a soil-forming factor in American thinking. He and {{ref:soil-hist-022}} greatly influenced {{ref:soil-hist-009}}, turning him from geology toward soil science as a distinct field.

soil-hist-009.title: Curtis Marbut builds the first US soil classification
soil-hist-009.text: Curtis F. Marbut began as a geologist who saw soils as surface reflections of the rock beneath. He ended by giving the United States its first formal soil classification. The American soil scientist (1863–1935) directed the Soil Survey Division of the US Department of Agriculture from 1913 until his death. Hilgard and {{ref:soil-hist-022}} helped turn him toward soil science as a field distinct from geology. He began the classification work in 1920. In 1927 he translated Glinka's The Great Soil Groups of the World and their Development into English, and he applied the Russian ideas to a national scheme. It became the 1935 system, modified and published in the 1938 Yearbook of Agriculture as the 1938 USDA soil taxonomy. At its highest level it split soils in two. Pedocals were carbonate-rich soils of drier climates; pedalfers were rich in aluminum and iron. "Alfer" became the root of alfisol. He died of pneumonia in 1935, on his way to advise the Chinese Geological Survey on organizing a soil survey.

soil-hist-023.title: Lorenzo Richards measures the water in soil
soil-hist-023.text: Lorenzo A. Richards (1904–1993) helped move the study of soil water from description to measurement and mathematics. The American was one of the most influential figures in 20th-century soil physics. His 1931 Cornell thesis on capillary conduction through porous media made the first decisive advance beyond Buckingham in extending Darcy's law to unsaturated soils. In it he set out the partial differential equation now called the {{ref:soil-water-238}}, though Lewis Richardson had published it in 1922. Richards described the principles, construction and operation of the tensiometer. He proposed the tension plate apparatus for measuring capillary potential in soil. In 1941 he described the pressure-membrane apparatus, mainly for extracting soil solution for salinity analysis. At the USDA Salinity Laboratory he and colleagues fixed the accepted limits for plant growth. Field capacity sits at −1/3 bar (−33 J/kg) and the permanent wilting point at −15 bar (−1500 J/kg). Yet he remarked that the concept of available water is oversimplified.

soil-hist-005.title: Minerals, not humus: how plants really feed
soil-hist-005.text: For a long time, many believed plants ate decayed plant matter. That humus theory held that humus was plants' main carbon source and that fertilizers worked by breaking it down. The mineral theory of plant nutrition said otherwise. Plants draw essential nutrients as inorganic minerals from the soil, and carbon and hydrogen from air and water. De Saussure's experiments of 1804 had suggested that plants took carbon from the air and that their mineral content reflected the soil they grew in. By the late 1830s {{ref:soil-hist-072}} had used Liebig's combustion analysis to show that manures owed their value to their minerals. Liebig synthesized and promoted the theory. With more precise measurements, he showed that a soil's humus could not supply enough carbon for the plants growing on it. He named nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium as essential to plant growth. Inorganic materials, he held, could feed plants as well as organic ones. He also popularized the law of the minimum that Sprengel had stated: growth is limited by the scarcest essential resource, not by the total available.

soil-hist-024.title: Guy Smith and the making of Soil Taxonomy
soil-hist-024.text: More than 15 years of Guy D. Smith's work led to a soil classification that came to be used worldwide. The American soil scientist (1907–1981) originally developed the USDA system called Soil Taxonomy. After wartime service he joined the USDA. From 1946 he worked as a soil correlator for the Soil Conservation Service, and from 1952 as Director of Soil Survey Investigations. Tasked with developing a way to classify soils, he produced the first of seven iterations of the system. He developed it in collaboration with European soil scientists. It was made official in 1965 and published in 1975. After retiring in 1973 he advised international partners on applying Soil Taxonomy. He died in 1981 in Ghent, where he taught.

soil-hist-026.title: Rattan Lal and the carbon in farm soils
soil-hist-026.text: In Nigeria, between 1970 and 1987, Rattan Lal found that organic carbon and nutrients disappeared from soils after deforestation. He studied mulching, cover crops and no-till farming to restore them. The Indian-American soil scientist, born in 1944, is a pioneer of soil-centered farm management for food security and climate-resilient agriculture. His work departed from the 1970s reliance on commercial fertilizer. It showed how no-till, cover crops, residues, mulching and agroforestry rebuild degraded soils and sequester carbon. His most cited paper, in Science in 2004, was the first report that restoring soil organic matter both improves soil health and lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide. His models suggest that restoring soil health could by 2100 double global grain yield, cut the land used for grain by 30% and reduce fertilizer use. He founded the Rattan Lal Center for Carbon Management and Sequestration at Ohio State and launched the C-FARM carbon farming project in 2021. He was IUSS president in 2017–2018, won the Japan Prize in 2019 and the World Food Prize in 2020.

soil-hist-019.title: Hugh Hammond Bennett, crusader against erosion
soil-hist-019.text: Many of Hugh Hammond Bennett's colleagues held that soil was a resource that could never be exhausted. He spent his career arguing otherwise. Bennett (1881–1960) pioneered soil conservation in the United States and headed the federal erosion agency now called the {{ref:soil-hist-050}}. Working as a soil surveyor from 1903, he first linked soil quality and erosion in a 1905 Virginia survey. He came to see soil erosion as a serious problem for the planet. In 1928 he co-wrote the USDA's Soil Erosion: A National Menace, his most influential work. Congressman James P. Buchanan then secured funds in 1929 for erosion studies, and a 1930 amendment created soil erosion experiment stations whose sites Bennett chose. From September 1933 he directed the Soil Erosion Service. His Dust Bowl advocacy helped pass the act of 27 April 1935 creating the Soil Conservation Service, which he led until 1951. By May 1936, nearly 40,000 farmers in the hardest-hit Dust Bowl region had put 5.5 million acres under terraced and contour-listed cultivation. The Coon Creek Watershed Project in Wisconsin was the first of many watershed projects set up to show farmers how to conserve soil. The new service marked the US government's acceptance of interpreting soils for soil and water conservation. Bennett also helped form the Soil Conservation Society of America, now the Soil and Water Conservation Society.

soil-hist-074.title: John Bennet Lawes and the first artificial fertilizer
soil-hist-074.text: The world's oldest agricultural research facility began with manures tested on plants in pots. John Bennet Lawes started those trials at Rothamsted before leaving Oxford in 1832, and soon extended them to field crops. The English entrepreneur and agricultural scientist (1814–1900) founded the experimental farm that became {{ref:soil-hist-053}}. In 1842 he patented a manure made by treating phosphates with sulfuric acid. That superphosphate began the artificial fertilizer industry. From the following year he worked with Joseph Henry Gilbert for more than half a century on crop and animal-feeding experiments. The two jointly received the Royal Society's Royal Medal in 1867. In 1889 Lawes endowed the Lawes Agricultural Trust to keep the experimental farm going.

soil-hist-020.title: Franklin Hiram King, father of American soil physics
soil-hist-020.text: Franklin Hiram King (1848–1911) has been called the father of soil physics in the United States. As professor of agricultural physics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison from 1888 to 1902, he applied physics to agriculture, with his greatest impact on soil science. He studied water-holding capacity, plants' moisture needs, aeration, the movement of soil water and groundwater, and the draft of plows. At the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902 he found that nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yields. That undermined the views of bureau chief Milton Whitney, and King was forced to resign. He is best remembered for {{ref:soil-hist-021}}.
